Using old era bit style graphics, Earthtongue is a ecosystem simulator where you try to balance fungi and bugs who develop within an alien crater to create a self sustaining microcosm. You play as a non-physical consciousness who has limited ability to influence things using intervention points, which slowly accumulate over time as your micro world becomes more diverse. The end result is very interesting and reasonably enjoyable, but it can become frustrating at times.

I definitely like the approach of this game. While there is a little micromanaging, your interventions are limited until the next allotment, so you'll spend a fair amount of time just watching things develop, which can be adjusted for speed. While you develop your world, you have a research page which tells you aspects of things you've learned about how these little creatures live and see insight about your true nature.

As the name of the game is balance, you're going to find there's a rocky road to understanding what does what. You won't really be overwhelmed with choices for the most part, but if creatures don't live long enough (or don't develop at all), you can't really learn what you need to do. Because your interventions are limited and creating a lifeform creates a higher cost for a while if you want to do it again, it can become frustrating as some creatures are very hard to develop. Because some of them can die almost instantly, you don't get the opportunity to figure them out, and meanwhile, your world is developing, which can be inhospitable to certain things. This is something that galled me.

I'm all for trial and error, but I'm several hours in at this point and I still don't know why certain creatures won't thrive, what they will or will not eat, how they behave, etc... because they die almost immediately. If you can't learn from a forced trial and error approach, you don't really have any options and there's not a lot in the way of out of game guides for Earthtongue. Why do my wasps keep dying? How do I make use of the red mantis? Where do I plant pitcher plants successfully? Almost six hours in and I have still have some fast dying creatures with little explanation, because the research won't update until they've lived for around 7500 time units. I would have preferred some kind of clue on how at least to start with some of these creatures and then learn more as time went on.

Creatures aside, you must maintain a balance of nutrients in the soil versus that which is locked inside creatures/the air. I think this represents a type of carbon cycle. With your interventions, you can occasionally call down nutrients, rain to hydrate the land, wind to spread spores, etc. These things can happen without you, but they're very rare. One of the options feels a bit off putting however. The meteor option can be used to create ground based nutrients and break up piles of dead bodies/undesired creatures. Aesthetically, I feel like this is an odd method for adjusting balance however, since asteroids are more analgous to the evolutionary dominance and change of various creatures in real earth history, than anything to do with natural balance. Additionally, the meteor option either comes as a fiery ball which can be used to burn excess carcasses like an incinerator, or just a frozen iceball which creates a less ground impact to deliver nutrients. I didn't see any way to control the outcome of which type arrives, which was vexing. None of the other weather options have that issue.

Lastly, and this could just be the result of the world I managed while trying to learn the game- the breakdown cycle of creatures doesn't keep up well. Detrivores are often sluggish in their work, and while my roaches reproduced reasonably fast, my flies barely did. That felt non-intuitive. In time, there were more dead bodies piling up than all the detrivores and meteor drops could keep up with. My advice? Avoid using locusts and sundew molds as long as possible. They get out of control rapidly and little seems to get them under control. I have the option to use an expensive meteor shower to wreck my world down a bit, but I feel like that's an unsatisfying answer to my dilemma. But I get it... balance is hard. I just wish I had the ability to come into this more equipped with information than just guessing at times. Some creatures also seem more effective at their 'jobs' than others.

Generally, I liked the old school graphics and basic animations. The developments of the fungi were also very detailed as they grow and wither in a very telling way. You can also see the extent of water and nutrients in the soil with some subtle graphical touches. However, I would have changed the three fliers (wasps, locusts, and flies), as they use the same model with very small palette changes.

The music is nice. Simple relaxing quasi-Metroid-like ditties although they can get a little tedious after a while.

As a bonus, there's also mod support to try out new maps and designs, but know that there's only a few around. Still, it can keep things fresh.

Aside from the frustrating inability to learn things in game at times, I like Earthtongue and I wouldn't mind seeing more of it.

 There are 28 forms of life split evenly between fungi and bugs, and each behave in different ways that you will have to account for - some bugs and fungi will work well together, while other combinations will just destroy each other and often themselves in the process. Earthtongue is a curious little beast, and the glowing satisfaction of seeing a stable ecosystem take shape is matched only by the complete vexation when starting your first world and not understanding how anything does anything.

This isn't strictly a game, per se... Yes, there are achievements both ingame and on Steam, and some of them are even remarkably difficult to get and will require a fair amount of either tactical thinking or dumb luck (although it doesn't hurt to have both), but Earthtongue is by and large what you might call an "interactive screensaver". You make a few small adjustments, attempt to nurture a balanced world, and mostly just sit back and watch everything interact.

It's fairly simple; there aren't very many special interactions between species... There's one beetle that's immune to the grasping tendrils of a particular carnivorous mold, there's a moth that acts as a pollinator by spreading the spores of whatever plant it's just eaten, and there is of course an implementation of the horrifying Cordyceps fungus. For the most part, everything else reacts by either eating or ignoring whatever it comes across.

But even with these simple functions, remarkably complex ecosystems can arise and thrive. The wasp eats the fly and its body is turned into nutrients for the soil, the fungus consumes the nutrients and grows full stalks, the beetle eats the stalks and attacks the snail to defend its territory, and the body of the snail is eaten by a fly. All for your viewing pleasure!


The actual life cycle is a teensy bit bizarre (nutrient dust falls from the sky? What is this, a fish tank?), and by no means are all the basic lifeforms balanced properly (locusts... Oh god, locusts), but that's part of the appeal! You don't just come in with a cosmic blueprint and know exactly how an ecosystem works and how to put it together, you need to see the creatures and plants for yourself and watch how they interact and how they survive in different circumstances. Observe, experiment, observe again... Or just let nature run its course through random events and see if something sticks!


It's definitely "zen", and despite its small annoyances I found it to be a remarkably compelling experience. It's not for everyone, but if you've been looking for an ecosystem simulator to poke and look at... This is exactly it.

An extra bonus is the developer, who added a couple brand new modules (thus introducing entirely new ecosystems that you need to learn and understand in order to make them bloom) as well as workshop support for community-made modules that extend the game's lifespan immensely. And that's all after having said "I probably won't be working much on this anymore, so don't expect any big updates"!

Now excuse me while I add on a couple more worlds from the workshop and chill out while poking at the natural economics of alien plants and animals...

Earthtongue is, more-or-less, a puzzle game.  It's one of those games where learning the rules to the game basically IS the game.  Hence, whether you'll like it probably depends on if you're the inquisitive sort that enjoys trying to experiment in games.  

You play with an alien landscape that, in the default world, is dark grey when dry but blue when wet, and has small white specks in the dirt to represent nutrients.  (It took me a while to figure that out while playing...)  You interact with the world by either rearranging existing insects (including corpses) or airborne spores (rooted fungi are unmovable), which is free, or by using gradually recharging "intervention" points to spawn new creatures or 'weather' events.  You generally want to keep the creatures alive, as not only is respawning creatures that go extinct costly, but you only get the diary entries that give you additional information if you can keep them alive for a significant period of time. 

Fungi need water and nutrients from the soil, and can deplete the soil of both (a common, cheap intervention makes it rain or drops nutrients, and this is by far my most common intervention), although different breeds consume different amounts of either.  Some are even like venus flytraps, and eat insects, while needing little nutrients.  

Insects, meanwhile, can eat fungi, hunt other insects, or scavenge the dead. Herbivores will vacuum up every last fungus if you aren't careful, while overbreeding to absolutely insane degrees.  

Spiders are my personal favorite, here.  Their communal webs are so interesting, and they help keep some of the more annoyingly voracious insects in check, but too many winds up making cone beetles take over to the point that cone beetle corpses are literally piled up in all the valleys to form bridges across.  

Considering the low price, and how unusual its premise is, it's well worth throwing down a couple dollars just for the sheer novelty factor. Keeping in mind that the point is to make the ecosystem as close to self-sufficient as possible, it can be a good game for when you aren't at 100% mentally, such as when feeling ill, but still want to do something semi-interactive.

I wasnt sure whether to reccomend this.  Though enjoyable, I'm not sure I would call earthtongue a game either.

Earthtongue does what it does well, and that is simulate environments. If that sounds like your cup of tea, just buy the damn thing. There are some bugs, most of which can be solved merely by changing to an older version of the game and turning on full screen. Upon returning to the current version, all should be fine. 


As I already said, not exactly a game. This is primarily because there is little interaction. Little is a relative term in this instance, so that is kind of debatable though. You can single handedly destroy and create environments, yes, but the point system, I feel, leaves a lot to be desired. That said, I quite enjoy just leaving the game running while I do pixel art in another tab. When I hit a wall, I just head on back to the game and see whats popping. Much to my surprise, a new species may have taken over.

I find it agitating that terraforming can not be done for free, and even more agitating that caves are not to be found. That said, a lot of the game is based on the weather and caves complicate that quite a bit. For the pricetag this is easily overlooked. 

More general polish, a faster timespeed(not too fast though), slightly cheaper critters, and more dependence on the weather would all be greatly appreciated and make the game much more enjoyable. Those are the only things I feel are real problems, and polish isnt so much a problem as it is nice.

Earthtongue is a cute game with a dirt cheap pricetag. There isnt much more to say. Earthtongue is, in a way, a basebuilding game. Except there are no enemies, just participants.
This is a delightful zen garden of a game. Nice to relax on a stress free afternoon while your favorite podcast plays on in the background. Can't recommend a casual experience like this enough.

Less a "game" in the traditional sense and more a toy like SimEarth this title will be most enjoyable to people who like to have something to play with, without necessarily having to pay a lot of attention to it.
A difficult, but fun little management game.

I recommend this game for the following reasons:

Meditative.

Thought provoking.

Great music.

You will most likely end up spending ages ensuring your favorite species flourishes, feeding corpses to your favored plants, and throwing carnivores away from your poor herbivores.

Also the mod-worlds are very wonderful and worth mentioning, including an earth preserve (OMG ADORABLE BUNNIES), metroid planet, mad scientist world, etc.
Great sandbox game, fun to explore and mess around with!
